title: 11+ Exam Formats: Why the Target School Matters
description: Why 11+ preparation should start with the target school and current admissions test. Understand how formats can differ, with GL Assessment and ISEB examples.

children: One of the easiest ways to waste 11+ preparation time is to practise a format simply because a workbook says “11+” on the cover. There is no single national paper. The subjects, timing, question balance and delivery method can vary by area, consortium and school.
Start with the admissions source, not the workbook

Before building a detailed preparation plan, check the current admissions information published by the target school, consortium or local authority. That should determine which skills and formats deserve the most attention.
Which subjects are tested?
Is the test paper-based or online?
Is it multiple choice, written response or a mixture?
Are verbal and non-verbal reasoning included?
Are there school-specific stages, interviews or additional written papers?
What are the current timings and test dates?
GL Assessment: a common example

GL Assessment provides 11+ materials across English, maths, verbal reasoning and non-verbal reasoning, but its own guidance warns that local tests can differ in timing, subjects and number of questions. Familiarisation is therefore useful, but it should not be mistaken for a guarantee that every local test is identical.
ISEB Common Pre-Tests: a different model

For pupils applying to schools using the ISEB Common Pre-Tests, the format is different again. The current tests are adaptive, online and multiple choice across English, mathematics, verbal reasoning and non-verbal reasoning, with a total testing time of 2 hours 15 minutes.

That means preparation for ISEB should include secure curriculum knowledge, reasoning familiarity and comfort working accurately in an adaptive online environment rather than simply completing generic paper packs.
What should stay the same across formats?
Strong reading accuracy and vocabulary.
Secure arithmetic and mathematical reasoning.
The ability to infer from evidence rather than guess.
Careful attention to instructions.
Gradually improving speed without sacrificing accuracy.
The ability to learn from mistakes rather than merely count scores.
When should preparation become test-specific?

Early preparation can concentrate on transferable foundations. As the exam approaches and the child’s basic skills become more secure, practice should increasingly resemble the actual test they will sit.
The closer the exam gets, the less useful it is to spend time on question types that do not appear in the target format.
How tuition should use this information

A tutor should know the target school or local test before claiming that preparation is “exam specific”. Current admissions details can then shape the balance of English, maths, reasoning, timing and interview preparation.
